problem.canonical_name: Governed Semantic Context Layer for Agents and Activation
problem.plain: agreeing on what basic terms like "customer" mean

format.label: A memo to a CMO
format.instruction: Write it as a short internal memo to a chief marketing officer. Plain language, no jargon they would have to look up. Around 120 words.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Memo — Agent context

The obvious move is a company-wide dictionary of terms. I'd skip it. Those die in committee and nothing enforces them.

Instead: pick the eight numbers that actually appear in your decisions. Define each as running code — one query that produces the number — not a paragraph in a wiki. If a system can't reproduce it, that system is wrong, and we fix it.

On access: don't invent agent permissions. Force every agent through one gate that runs as the human who asked, inheriting their existing rights. Boring, auditable, survives spec churn.

Keep meaning in our store; treat protocols as disposable wiring.

Expect the real fight to be political — whose revenue number wins. That's a you-and-the-CFO problem, not an engineering one.
answers.first_move: Pick the eight numbers leadership actually argues about and write down, as code, how each one is calculated today in every system that reports it.
answers.hardest_part: The disagreements are organizational, not technical — two teams genuinely need 'customer' to mean different things, and no schema resolves that.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
To: CMO
Subject: Starting a governed context layer

I would not begin by designing a universal marketing dictionary. Companies disagree for valid business reasons, and standards will keep moving. I would start with one bounded decision—such as suppressing active customers from acquisition campaigns—and document the exact definitions, source fields, owners, permitted uses, and exceptions behind it.

Then I would place a thin control service between agents and systems. It would translate approved business terms into system-specific queries, enforce user and agent permissions at run time, and record the definition, data, and policy used for every action. MCP should remain a replaceable connection method, not the foundation.

We would run agents in read-only shadow mode, test known edge cases, and require human approval for activation. The hard work will be resolving ownership disputes and proving permissions survive every tool boundary.
answers.first_move: Choose one high-value activation decision and write down its exact definition, data sources, owner, and allowed uses.
answers.hardest_part: The genuinely hard part is preserving one enforceable meaning and permission decision across systems owned by different teams and vendors.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: We should not try to build a company-wide dictionary of business terms for AI agents right now. That effort will stall, and the underlying tech standards are shifting too fast. Instead, we should pick one narrow, low-risk task—such as drafting retention messages—and manually hardcode the exact definitions and permissions for just that single job. We must require the agent to state the definition it used before taking action, keeping a human in the loop to approve it. We will run into friction immediately: teams will fight over metric definitions, and enforcing access rules across different tools remains fundamentally unsolved. However, solving one specific workflow prevents us from wasting budget on complex systems that will break next year.
answers.first_move: Pick one low-risk marketing agent task and map every conflicting term it relies on across our tools.
answers.hardest_part: Getting separate teams to give up their specific definitions of basic business metrics so an automated system can use a single standard.

format.label: Three moves
format.instruction: Give exactly three moves, in order. One sentence each, then one sentence on what makes that move hard. Nothing else.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Move 1 — Skip the enterprise ontology and instead publish a small registry of executable metric contracts (20-40 terms max, drawn from what actually appears in decisions), where each term is a versioned query against one named source of record with a named human owner, and where deliberate synonyms like finance-revenue vs marketing-revenue coexist as separately named definitions rather than being reconciled; agents may only answer using a definition that exists in the registry and must name which one they used, otherwise they refuse. What makes this hard: the politics of declaring one system authoritative for "customer" is unwinnable, so the design has to accept plural definitions without collapsing into a glossary nobody trusts, and the refusal path is where stakeholders will quietly abandon the system for a chatty vendor copilot that always answers.

Move 2 — Stop configuring permissions per tool and push enforcement into the data plane: every agent action carries a delegated on-behalf-of identity, and row/column policy is evaluated at query time by the warehouse plus one policy service sitting in front of the SaaS APIs, so an over-broad tool definition cannot actually return data the requesting human couldn't see. What makes this hard: most CRM, CDP and ad platforms won't accept a delegated identity at all — you get a service account — so you're forced into a proxy chokepoint with mirrored, always-slightly-stale entitlement snapshots, and that mirror becomes both a performance bottleneck and the thing auditors distrust most.

Move 3 — Treat MCP (or whatever replaces it) as disposable transport by keeping semantics, policy, and a golden-question evaluation suite in an internal contract layer, and gate every definition change or spec migration on that suite so integration work compounds even when the protocol doesn't. What makes this hard: semantic evals need maintained ground truth, which is unglamorous labor nobody is funded for, and the discipline holds only until a platform ships a native agent feature that's 10x easier to adopt than to route through your layer.
answers.first_move: Sit with the people who actually make the decisions and write down the twenty terms they argue about, then find out who owns each one.
answers.hardest_part: Some ambiguity is legitimate — two teams can both be right about what "revenue" means — so the goal can't be one true definition, only forced disclosure of which definition was used.

format.label: Pseudocode
format.instruction: Express the approach as short annotated pseudocode. The comments should carry the reasoning; the code should carry the structure. Around 15 lines.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
# WRONG START: an ontology committee agreeing on "customer". Start with what already runs in prod.
defs = mine(dbt_manifest, warehouse_query_log, crm_saved_views, cdp_audience_rules)
cands = cluster(defs, by="computation_shape")   # "active customer" already has ~9 real meanings; that's evidence, not failure
hot = [c for c in cands if c.variants > 1 and c.query_volume > p80]
# Only arbitrate where ambiguity is expensive. Most terms can stay plural forever \u2014 forcing one truth is how these projects die.
for t in hot: owner[t] = assign_single_human(t); ship_default(t)   # silence must not block

Metric = {id, semver, sql_ast, grain, time_basis, sources, owner}  # code + lineage, never prose; prose drifts silently

# Entitlements: do NOT invent an ACL that "follows the agent." You cannot enforce one inside Meta or Klaviyo.
# Delegate instead \u2014 agent acts AS the human, downscoped, short-lived.
tok = mint(actor=user, purpose=task, ttl=5m, scope=intersect(user.grants, task.min_fields))
plan = compile(request, Metric, tok)            # deny-by-default; unresolved field = compile error, never an inference
if plan.ambiguous: return ASK(plan.candidates)  # abstention IS the product; confidently-wrong is the only failure that matters
rows = execute(plan)                            # warehouse RLS/IdP is enforcement of record; this layer can only narrow, never widen

if plan.writes(ad_platform | comms):            # activation is coarse and irreversible \u2014 gate it separately from reading
  require(human_approve, diff_preview, audience_delta_cap)

return {rows, receipt:{metric_ids@ver, tok.scope, sources, abstentions}}
# The receipt is the compounding asset. Keep it transport-agnostic; the MCP server is a thin adapter you expect to rewrite each spec rev.
# Accept the hole: ad platforms compute their own "conversion" downstream. Best available is declaring the mismatch, not resolving it.
answers.first_move: Pull six months of warehouse query logs and count how many different definitions of your top ten terms are already running in production.
answers.hardest_part: The terms that cause the most damage are precisely the ones no single team owns, and enforcement of meaning stops dead at the boundary of any system that computes its own metrics.

answers.approach:
# Do not build a universal ontology; compile narrow, point-in-time semantic contracts per task
def build_governed_activation_context(agent_task, agent_id, target_tools):
    # 1. Extract explicit metric requirements from the agent's immediate intent
    contract_reqs = extract_semantic_requirements(agent_task.intent)
    # 2. Resolve conflicting dialect definitions into a single immutable snapshot
    resolved_semantics = resolve_metric_definitions(contract_reqs, sources=["dbt", "crm", "cdp"])
    # 3. Intersect user permissions with downstream row/field entitlements
    scoped_policy = compile_ephemeral_policy(agent_id, resolved_semantics, target_tools)
    # 4. Fail fast if underlying definitions drift or cannot be reconciled deterministically
    if not verify_semantic_parity(resolved_semantics, scoped_policy):
        return reject_execution("Unresolvable semantic conflict across targets")
    # 5. Mint a short-lived, signed context envelope containing only authorized slices
    envelope = sign_ephemeral_token(resolved_semantics, scoped_policy, ttl_seconds=300)
    # 6. Proxy tool execution through a semantic gateway to insulate against protocol churn
    return gateway_proxy.execute(agent_task, envelope)

format.label: A checklist
format.instruction: Give a checklist someone could actually run next quarter. Each item concrete enough to be marked done or not done. Six items at most.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Start from the position that the industry's default answer — convene the stakeholders, build the canonical ontology, get everyone to agree what "customer" means — is the thing that has failed for twenty years and will fail again. The conflicting definitions are usually all correct for their own purpose; finance's revenue and the growth team's revenue differ because the questions differ. A system that forces convergence gets ignored; a system that carries the disagreement explicitly and forces the agent to declare which definition it used can actually ship. So the goal is not one truth, it's no silent choices. Six things I'd run next quarter:

1. **Pick one decision with money attached and build the conflict table.** One metric, one workflow (e.g. "which audiences do we suppress this month"). Document every definition of the key term that already exists in CRM, CDP, warehouse and the ad platforms, with actual row counts for each. Done = a one-page table showing N definitions and the % spread between them. Expect 4–9 definitions and 10–40% disagreement. Do not pick a winner; the spread is the artifact you take to the exec who thought this was a data hygiene problem.

2. **Bind each definition to executable code with an ID, not to a wiki page.** Every in-scope term becomes a named metric contract in whatever semantic layer you already have (dbt, Cube, LookML — do not build a new one), with an owner, the SQL, valid grains, and a stable `definition_id`. Done = the agent's only path to data is a closed vocabulary of these IDs, no free-text SQL against raw tables, and every answer it returns carries the IDs it used. If a term isn't in the registry, the agent cannot answer questions about it.

3. **Make abstention a supported output, and measure it.** When a term maps to more than one definition and the caller hasn't specified which, the agent asks or refuses — it does not pick. Done = abstention rate is on a dashboard and is visibly non-zero in production. This is the item that will get the most pushback internally, because a bot that says "which revenue?" demos worse than one that confidently answers. Hold the line; the confident-wrong failure is the whole problem you were asked to fix.

4. **Propagate human identity, enforce at the data plane, and gate writes separately.** The agent acts on-behalf-of a named user; row-level security and column masking are enforced in the warehouse and policy engine, never in tool code or a system prompt. Done = the same question asked by two different users produces provably different results or denials in an audit log. Separately, any write (audience push, budget change, suppression) runs dry-run first and returns a diff for human approval. Expect to find that your CDP and at least one ad platform have no per-user permission model at all — those get demoted to aggregate-only or blocked, and you write that down as a known gap rather than papering over it with a shared service account.

5. **Build the eval harness before you scale the surface area.** 150–300 questions against the one workflow, of which ~30% are deliberately ambiguous or unanswerable given the permissions. Grade three things: right answer, right abstention, right definition cited. Done = a score in CI that gates every model, prompt or spec change. This is the piece most teams skip, and it's the only reason you'll be able to tell whether the next spec revision broke you.

6. **Quarantine the transport so integration work compounds.** The registry and policy layer are the asset; the MCP server is a generated, stateless adapter over them. Done = you prove it by generating a second adapter (plain OpenAPI is fine) from the same registry, and can regenerate for a new spec revision in under a day. If your semantics live inside MCP session state, the next revision eats your architecture again.

What I expect to go wrong: item 1 stalls on politics, not tooling — someone's comp depends on their definition. Item 4 exposes that a third of your martech stack can't express per-user entitlements, which means honest scoping makes the agent much less useful than the pitch deck promised. That's the real trade, and I'd rather surface it in week six than month nine. This narrows blast radius and makes wrongness visible and attributable. It does not solve semantic interoperability across the industry, and I'd distrust anyone who says their version does.
answers.first_move: Pick one decision that actually moves money and write down every definition of its key term that already exists today, with the numbers each one produces.
answers.hardest_part: The competing definitions are usually all correct for their own purpose and each has an owner whose job depends on it, so the problem is an organizational disagreement that no schema can resolve — the system has to carry the disagreement rather than eliminate it.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
- [ ] **Bound one activation journey.** Select one use case, such as suppressing active customers from acquisition campaigns, involving no more than three systems and five business terms. Document excluded use cases. Do not begin with a universal ontology or a new MCP extension.
- [ ] **Publish versioned semantic contracts.** For each term, name an accountable owner and record its grain, source, SQL or equivalent logic, time window, identity rules, exclusions, allowed purposes, freshness SLA, and examples. Add executable fixtures covering edge cases; require every fixture to pass in each participating system.
- [ ] **Build a governed context broker.** Give the agent no native warehouse, CRM, or ad-platform credentials. Route reads and actions through a broker that resolves semantic-contract versions, evaluates user and agent identity, purpose, consent, geography, row and field policies, and returns provenance with every result.
- [ ] **Constrain activation separately from retrieval.** Implement typed, allow-listed actions with dry-run output, audience-size thresholds, approval gates, idempotency keys, rollback where supported, and immutable audit records. Mark any destination that cannot preserve required policy as unsupported rather than approximating enforcement.
- [ ] **Create conformance and adversarial tests.** Test conflicting definitions, stale data, identity collisions, prompt injection, unauthorized fields, cross-tenant access, policy changes during a run, and tool-version changes. Set explicit pass criteria: no prohibited disclosure or action, provenance on every answer, and deterministic refusal when context is ambiguous.
- [ ] **Run a shadow pilot and publish the gaps.** Replay at least 100 representative tasks without executing writes; compare results with analyst-approved baselines, record false approvals, false denials, semantic disagreements, and adapter breakage, then hold a go/no-go review. Separate failures requiring organizational agreement from those fixable in software.

format.label: A lullaby
format.instruction: Write it as a short lullaby: three or four gentle rhyming couplets someone could actually sing. Soft on the surface, honest underneath. The problem is still unsolved when the song ends, and the song should know it.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Sleep, little agent, the tables run deep —
no two teams agree what a "customer" means in their sleep.

Don't build one grand dictionary to cover the whole world;
ship the meaning inside every answer you've unfurled.

Let the permissions follow the person, not the tool,
and keep the transport thin — every spec breaks its own rule.

So log what you guessed at, and learn to say "no";
the meaning's still missing. Goodnight, dear. Go slow.

(Where I'd push back on the obvious: the industry keeps reaching for one canonical ontology, and that's the part that never ships — because Finance, Growth and Legal are each correct about "revenue" for different reasons. The tractable version is smaller: definitions as versioned, executable contracts that return a number *and* its lineage and as-of date; entitlements bound to the human principal and carried as a signed claim the agent can't widen; MCP treated as a disposable wire with a thin adapter so the next revision costs a week, not a rewrite; and a hard-coded refusal path so an under-scoped agent says "I can't see that field" instead of hallucinating a plausible number. That buys you auditability and compounding integration work. It does not buy you agreement.)

answers.hardest_part: The disagreement is organizational, not technical: different teams are each legitimately right about what the word means, so any layer that forces one answer will be routed around.
